what_its_for: Anidulafungin is an antifungal medicine used to treat serious fungal infections caused by a yeast called Candida. It can treat infections in your blood (called candidemia), in your belly area, or in your food pipe (esophagus). This medicine works by stopping the fungus from growing and spreading in your body.
how_to_take: Anidulafungin is given as a slow drip into your vein (intravenous or IV infusion) by a nurse or doctor in a hospital or clinic setting. You will not give this medicine to yourself at home in most cases. Each dose is given over at least 90 minutes to 3 hours depending on the dose. Never receive this infusion faster than your doctor or nurse has ordered, as it can cause serious reactions.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on the type of infection you have. A common starting dose for blood or serious infections is 200 mg on the first day, then 100 mg once daily after that. For esophageal (food pipe) infections, the starting dose is usually 100 mg on the first day, then 50 mg once daily. Treatment usually lasts at least 14 days or longer depending on how well you respond. Always follow your doctor's instructions exactly.
missed_dose: Since this medicine is given by a healthcare provider in a clinical setting, a missed dose should be rescheduled as soon as possible. Contact your doctor or clinic right away if you miss or need to reschedule an appointment. Do not try to double up doses to make up for a missed one.
storage: Anidulafungin is stored and prepared by healthcare professionals. Unopened vials should be kept in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Once the medicine is mixed and ready to be given as an infusion, it should be used within 48 hours if kept at room temperature or within 72 hours if refrigerated. Do not freeze the prepared solution.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor about all medicines you take before starting this medication, including over-the-counter drugs, vitamins, and herbal supplements. Although anidulafungin has fewer drug interactions than some other antifungals, it is still important to disclose everything. Avoid stopping treatment early even if you feel better, as the infection may come back. Do not take more or less than prescribed.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or get medical help right away if you experience any of the following during or after your infusion: flushing (redness or warmth of the skin), rash or hives, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, difficulty breathing or chest tightness, low blood pressure or feeling faint, fast or irregular heartbeat, nausea, vomiting, or severe stomach pain, yellowing of the skin or eyes (signs of liver problems), or dark urine. Also tell your doctor if your symptoms do not improve after a few days of treatment.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within the first few days of treatment, but it is very important to complete the full course of treatment your doctor has prescribed. The full treatment usually lasts at least 14 days for blood or serious infections. Stopping too early can allow the fungal infection to come back or become harder to treat.
special_populations: Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. The safety of anidulafungin during pregnancy has not been fully established, so your doctor will weigh the risks and benefits. Children: Anidulafungin may be used in some children, but the dose will be adjusted based on the child's weight. Your doctor will determine if this is appropriate. Older Adults: Older patients generally do not need a dose adjustment, but should be monitored closely. Kidney or Liver Disease: No dose adjustment is typically needed for kidney problems. Patients with severe liver disease should be monitored closely by their doctor.
